classification.difficultyReason: Combine rotational symmetry, Pythagoras and correctly ordered similar triangles to establish the central triangle's area ratio.

content.prompt: $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral, $X$ is on $AB$ and $AX:XB=1:2$. $Y$ is on $BC$ and $BY:YC=1:2$. $Z$ is on $CA$ and $CZ:ZA=1:2$. $AY$, $BZ$ and $CX$ intersect at $P$, $Q$ and $R$. Prove that the area of $\triangle PQR$ is one-seventh of the area of $\triangle ABC$.

spec.description: Unfilled equilateral triangle with three cevians and all nine source labels. Ordinary source-blue linework is reconstructed in house black. No new measurement, equality or angle marks are supplied.
spec.mathematics: AX:XB=BY:YC=CZ:ZA=1:2; P=AY∩BZ, Q=AY∩CX, R=BZ∩CX. Coordinates derive each intersection exactly.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source geometry and labels are visible; the area ratio and proof remain hidden.

answer.short:
$\operatorname{area}(\triangle PQR)=\dfrac17\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)$.

Rotational symmetry makes $PQR$ equilateral. Similarity and Pythagoras give its side-length ratio to $ABC$ as $1:\sqrt7$, so its area ratio is $1:7$.
answer.worked:
Choose the side length of $ABC$ as $1$ unit; this does not change an area ratio. Then $AX=BY=CZ=\tfrac13$.

A rotation of $120^\circ$ about the centre sends $A\to C\to B\to A$, $X\to Z\to Y\to X$ and $Q\to R\to P\to Q$. Hence $PQR$ is equilateral, $AQ=CR=BP$, and $AY=BZ=CX$.

Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $Z$ to $BC$. Since $\angle ZCM=60^\circ$, $CM=\tfrac16$. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}ZM^2&=CZ^2-CM^2\\ZM^2&=\left(\frac13\right)^2-\left(\frac16\right)^2\\ZM^2&=\frac1{12},\\BM&=1-\frac16=\frac56,\\BZ^2&=BM^2+ZM^2\\BZ^2&=\frac{25}{36}+\frac1{12}\\BZ^2&=\frac79,\\BZ&=\frac{\sqrt7}{3}.\end{align*}$$
The same rotation gives $\angle BYP=\angle CZB$. Also $\angle PBY=\angle CBZ$, since $B,P,Z$ are collinear and $B,Y,C$ are collinear. Therefore $\triangle BPY\sim\triangle BCZ$ by AAA, in matching order.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BP}{BC}&=\frac{PY}{CZ}=\frac{BY}{BZ}\\\frac{BY}{BZ}&=\frac{1/3}{\sqrt7/3}=\frac1{\sqrt7},\\BP&=\frac1{\sqrt7},\\PY&=\frac1{3\sqrt7}.\end{align*}$$
Since $AQ=BP$ and $A,Q,P,Y$ occur in that order on $AY$,
$$\begin{align*}PQ&=AY-AQ-PY\\PQ&=\frac{\sqrt7}{3}-\frac1{\sqrt7}-\frac1{3\sqrt7}\\PQ&=\frac1{\sqrt7}.\end{align*}$$
Both $PQR$ and $ABC$ are equilateral, so they are similar. Thus
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\operatorname{area}(\triangle PQR)}{\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)}&=\left(\frac{PQ}{AB}\right)^2\\\frac{\operatorname{area}(\triangle PQR)}{\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)}&=\left(\frac1{\sqrt7}\right)^2\\\frac{\operatorname{area}(\triangle PQR)}{\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)}&=\frac17.\end{align*}$$
